newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH TIMBER UNION EMBRACES ACADEMICS' JOBS PLAN.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH TIMBER UNION EMBRACES ACADEMICS' JOBS PLAN.

text.p: The wood workers' union said in a statement on Monday that job creation proposals by three economics experts outlined in daily Helsingin Sanomat newspaper on Sunday should be taken seriously.

"Although the programme goes beyond what is currently possible for the mechanical forest industry and the furniture industry, it could be implemented in the long term," union chairman Heikki Peltonen said in the statement.
The professors said Finland should boost employment by building two 1,000-megawatt nuclear power plants, two pulp mills, five paper machines and 100-150 wood chip power plants.

The three Helsinki School of Economics experts -- doctor of economics Heikki Urmas, chancellor Fedi Vaivio and rector Veikko Jaaskelainen -- said such a programme would generate 250,000 new jobs during the building phase, and 120,000 jobs would become permanent.

Funds from the privatisation of state-controlled companies should be used to partly finance the programme, the experts said. They estimated the proceeds to the state from such share sales at around 50 billion markka over the next 10 years.
The programme's strong forest industry focus rests on the fact that annual new growth of Finnish forests at 80 million cubic metres exceeds annual cuttings by 25 million cubic metres.

The wood workers' union said the government should appoint a broad-based panel of experts to draft concrete proposals based on the programme. Starting to implement the programme would show that political decision-makers are really serious about fighting unemployment, union chairman Peltonen said.
The same programme was supported by metal workers' union chairman Per-Erik Lundh in a speech in November.
Lundh and Peltonen are among the most influential member union leaders of the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK).

SAK has repeatedly said that improved employment is a key condition for its support for the government's drive to put Finland in the first wave of countries to join the third stage of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in 1999.
SAK is expected to decide its stance on EMU next autumn.
Political analysts say it would be very difficult for MPs of pro-EMU Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's Social Democratic Party to vote for Finnish EMU membership if SAK were opposed.
In a weekend interview in a regional newspaper, Lipponen said the SDP party council would rule for or against Finnish EMU membership in the autumn.
The Finnish parliament will vote on the EMU issue early in 1998, Lipponen said.

SDP is the biggest party in parliament and in the left-right-green government, which upon taking office in April 1995 set as its most important task to halve unemployment to 8-9 percent by the end of its term in 1999.
So far, unemployment has fallen very slowly.

Most economists agree that the jobless rate will not be halved by 1999 through the measures currently in use despite the strong pace of economic growth -- up to four percent -- expected this year by the finance ministry, the central bank and some leading economic research institutes.
Helsingin Sanomat noted that it could be very difficult for the government and parliament to decide to build new nuclear power plants. The Green Party would almost certainly walk out.
